flashcards.a: A bounded routing layer: generate a small candidate set, score capability fit, abstain below a calibrated threshold, and invoke a worker only after selection. Availability fallback is a separate bounded path after a classified failure.

flashcards.q: Why bound the candidate set before scoring?
flashcards.a: A full catalog recreates over-tooling: attention is diluted, schemas consume context, and selection is harder to measure. Candidate generation must also be measured for correct-candidate recall at k.

flashcards.q: What is the lab's confidence formula?
flashcards.a: Coverage is top overlap divided by required-skill count; separation is (top overlap minus runner-up overlap) divided by top overlap; confidence is coverage times separation. No match has zero confidence.

flashcards.q: What must happen below the confidence threshold?
flashcards.a: Abstain before invoking a worker. Return an explicit result and use a safe path such as clarification, human review, or a constrained single-agent baseline.

flashcards.q: Routing versus fallback: what is the distinction?
flashcards.a: Routing is predictive selection based on capability or difficulty. Fallback is reactive availability handling after a timeout, 429, 5xx, overload, or refusal. They need different metrics and budgets.
Only classified availability failures. Invalid input, policy denial, malformed output from a contract bug, and unexpected exceptions should not be hidden by trying another worker.

flashcards.q: How do you account for fallback cost and latency?
flashcards.a: Charge every attempted candidate before dispatch. Total cost is token count times the sum of attempted candidate prices; total latency includes every attempted round trip, including the failed primary.

Confidence predicts capability fit; authorization decides whether the candidate may perform the action. Authorization must be enforced below the model against actual tool parameters, regardless of route confidence.
Route accuracy against labels, candidate-set recall, route distribution, abstention quality, fallback rate, quality by route, and cost/latency by route, all correlated in one trace.

flashcards.q: How do you prove orchestration beats one agent?
flashcards.a: Use the same golden tasks and comparable tools and budget, then compare quality, route metrics, tokens, p50/p95/p99 latency, and cost against a single-agent baseline, including a same-budget single-agent comparison.

For parallel read-heavy work, mandatory context isolation, different permission/trust tiers, different model/latency tiers, independent deployment ownership, or untrusted-content quarantine. Tool count alone is not sufficient.

flashcards.q: What is the evidence status of Instagram-derived material in this module?
flashcards.a: Instagram is discovery-only: it can reveal a curriculum gap but is not technical evidence. Claims are grounded in the cited curriculum modules and primary or official sources listed in the module.
